explanation.overall:
The key detector landed on C major, but only at 64% confidence — and that hesitation is the whole song. Dreams rocks between two chords for four minutes (from my knowledge of the record, F and G), and both of them lean toward C without ever playing it. Every bar poses a question the song declines to answer. That's why it survives with no bridge, no key change, no chorus that lifts to a new chord, and still doesn't feel stuck: it isn't going anywhere on purpose. Wanting someone doesn't resolve either.

With the harmony frozen, the arrangement has to supply all the motion, and the measurements show exactly how it does it. There are about 5 note attacks per second in the clip — roughly two and a half per beat at the measured 117 BPM — so the surface is genuinely busy while the chords sit dead still. Motion without travel. And the lifts are built from loudness and treble rather than chord changes: the clip's quietest point (0.30) sits four seconds before its loudest (0.81), and the final third is its brightest by a wide margin (1784 Hz average against 1317 in the middle third). Voices stack, cymbals open, nothing modulates.

The lyric runs the same play in words. Two verses with near-identical openings and one word swapped; a chorus that disguises a personal accusation as a weather report; an ending that repeats a promise instead of delivering one.

moments.moment: the swell with no chord change
moments.what_happens: Energy sinks to the clip's lowest reading (0.30 at 21.4s), then climbs to its highest (0.81 at 25.7s) — the largest sustained rise in the measured curve — and the clip's final third is also its brightest (1784 Hz average vs 1317 in the middle third).
moments.why_it_hits: It gets louder and higher without the ground moving underneath. The lift is pure texture — more voices, more cymbal — so the intensity rises while the harmony stays exactly where it was. That's the physical sensation of a feeling getting stronger without getting any closer to being over.

moments.what_happens: Verse two opens by rebuilding verse one's first line almost exactly, swapping 'here you go again' for 'here I go again' — and then she admits she keeps her visions to herself.
moments.why_it_hits: The kiss-off turns out to have been a self-portrait. You retroactively re-hear verse one as her describing her own restlessness, which means the whole opening accusation was a mirror she was holding at arm's length.

moments.what_happens: The chorus opens with a literal fact — 'thunder only happens when it's raining' — then reuses that exact grammar for a line about people who only love while they're playing at it.
moments.why_it_hits: Matched sentence shapes make the second claim inherit the first one's authority. She smuggles an opinion about him through as if it were meteorology, and there's nothing to argue with, which is far more wounding than shouting.

moments.what_happens: Verse lines arrive roughly 7–8 seconds apart, then between 0:58 and 1:11 four short lines alternate two phrases about having and losing at about 4-second intervals — the turnover doubles while the writing stops advancing.
moments.why_it_hits: You hear a mind snagged rather than a writer choosing. Speeding up into repetition, saying less faster, is what rumination actually feels like from the inside — and the two-chord loop underneath means nothing arrives to break the spiral.

moments.moment: seventeen seconds with no one in it
moments.what_happens: After the first chorus the vocal vanishes from 1:42 to 2:00 while the band keeps the same two-chord vamp turning over, unchanged.
moments.why_it_hits: The song demonstrates that it runs perfectly well without her in it. The loop doesn't falter, doesn't miss the voice — which is precisely the fear the lyric just finished describing.

explanation.lyric_read: The writing works by repetition with one small mutation, which is harder than it sounds. Verse two rebuilds verse one and changes a pronoun, so the song reveals itself as a confession rather than a complaint. The chorus pairs an unarguable fact about rain with a sentence shaped identically that is entirely her verdict, and the matched grammar makes the verdict feel like physics. Notice what's withheld: no name, no incident, no specific charge — just conditions, the way you describe weather. The one concrete offer is oddly archaic, asking whether he has any dreams he'd like to sell, which turns love into a market stall and her into someone bidding on scraps. Even the tempo backs the imagery: the lyric at 0:48 describes a heartbeat driving you mad, and the measured pulse is 117 BPM — an agitated heart rate, not a resting one. Then the last twenty-odd seconds just repeat a two-word promise four times and fade, never once telling us what he'll know.
explanation.headline: It rocks between two chords and never lands home — so the longing never resolves.

suggestions.title: Everybody Knows
suggestions.why: Builds an indictment out of a repeated declarative frame of unarguable statements, so a personal betrayal lands as a law of nature — the same trick as the thunder/players couplet.

suggestions.title: Tomorrow Never Knows
suggestions.why: Sits on a single unchanging chord for the entire track, forcing every rise and fall to come from texture and drums rather than harmony — Dreams' two-chord refusal taken one chord further.

suggestions.title: Ain't No Sunshine
suggestions.why: Its middle section abandons new lines and repeats one word dozens of times — repetition used as rumination, exactly like the had/lost loop where the lyric stops advancing and just circles.
